garamaudo:study:1.title: Garamaudo bauciensis, a new freshwater mosasaurid (Reptilia, Squamata) from the Santonian (Late Cretaceous) of Provence, southeastern France (Peer Community Journal, 2026)

garamaudo:abstract:1.title: Garamaudo bauciensis, a new freshwater mosasaurid (Reptilia, Squamata) from the Santonian (Late Cretaceous) of Provence, southeastern France (abstract)

facts.statement: Garamaudo lived during the Late Cretaceous Santonian age in freshwater rocks of France.
facts.quote: known from Late Cretaceous (Santonian age) rocks of France

facts.statement: The only species in the genus is Garamaudo bauciensis.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Garamaudo bauciensis

facts.statement: Garamaudo fossils were discovered in the Aix‑en‑Provence Basin at the Bouc‑Bel‑Air – Sousquières locality in southeastern France.
facts.quote: The Garamaudo fossil material was discovered in outcrops of the Aix-en-Provence Basin (Bouc-Bel-Air - Sousquières locality) in Bouc-Bel-Air, Bouches-du-Rhône department, in southeastern France.

facts.statement: The most complete specimen, designated the holotype, includes about 20 skeletal elements and was collected in 1997.
facts.quote: The most complete of these is CD13-PAL.2018.3.1–3, 5–15, 18, which comprises around 20 elements of a single individual collected by the Museum d'Histoire Naturelle Aix-en-Provence in 1997.

facts.statement: Garamaudo bauciensis is estimated to have been about 2.5 m long.
facts.quote: The total body length was likely around 2.5 m

facts.statement: Its limbs and pelvic girdle were more primitive and lacked the paddle‑like flippers of derived mosasaurids.
facts.quote: The limbs and pelvic girdle of Garamaudo may have been more plesiomorphic ('primitive') in morphology in contrast to the derived paddle-like flippers of other mosasaurids.

facts.statement: The fossils show clear osteosclerosis, indicating the animal could dive to shallow depths.
facts.quote: The known Garamaudo fossils exhibit clear osteosclerosis (increased bone density), indicating it was likely capable of diving to shallow depths.

facts.statement: Garamaudo probably captured prey by ambush rather than rapid acceleration.
facts.quote: It may not have been capable of rapid acceleration and maneuverability, instead catching prey by ambush.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Garamaudo in an unresolved clade within the subfamily Tethysaurinae, alongside Pannoniasaurus, Tethysaurus and an unnamed taxon.
facts.quote: It was recovered in an unresolved clade with Pannoniasaurus, Tethysaurus, and an unnamed taxon from Villeveyrac-L'Olivet, together forming the subfamily Tethysaurinae.

facts.statement: The generic name Garamaudo comes from the Provençal phrase meaning “beware the cursed one”.
facts.quote: The generic name, Garamaudo, is derived from the Provençal expression Gara au maudo, which means beware the cursed one

facts.statement: The specific epithet bauciensis refers to the type locality Bouc‑Bel‑Air.
facts.quote: The specific name, bauciensis, means from Bouc-Bel-Air, referencing the type locality.

facts.statement: Fish fossils from the locality include the gar Atractosteus africanus and the coelacanth Axelrodichthys megadromos.
facts.quote: Other fossils from the locality include fish, such as Atractosteus africanus (a gar) and Axelrodichthys megadromos (a coelacanth).

facts.statement: The description of Garamaudo bauciensis was published in Peer Community Journal in 2026 by Nathalie Bardet and colleagues.
facts.quote:
Journal: Peer Community Journal
Year: 2026
Authors: Nathalie Bardet, Alexandra Houssaye, François-Louis Pelissier, Yves Dutour, Eric Turini, Thierry Tortosa

facts.statement: Garamaudo is estimated to be about 2.5 m long and possessed limbs adapted for terrestrial locomotion and a sacrum, with osteosclerotic vertebrae and humerus.
